claims.claim: The page explains cloture and the Senate 60-vote threshold
claims.sourceSpan: is the only procedure by which the Senate can vote to set an end to a debate without also rejecting the bill, amendment, conference report, motion, or other matter it has been debating

claims.claim: Cloture is the only Senate rule that ends debate without rejecting the matter being debated
claims.sourceSpan: is the only procedure by which the Senate can vote to set an end to a debate without also rejecting the bill, amendment, conference report, motion, or other matter it has been debating

claims.claim: Rule XXII sets three thresholds
claims.sourceSpan: The majority required to invoke cloture for most business is three-fifths of the Senators duly chosen and sworn, or 60 votes if there are no vacancies in the Senate's membership. However, invoking cloture on a measure or motion to amend the Senate's standing rules requires the votes of two-thirds of the Senators present and voting, or 67 votes if all 100 Senators vote. Additionally, under precedents established on November 21, 2013, and April 6, 2017, invoking cloture on presidential nominations requires a vote of a majority of Senators present and voting, or 51 votes if all 100 Senators vote

claims.claim: A cloture motion takes sixteen signatures
claims.sourceSpan: signed by sixteen Senators

claims.claim: The 30-hour cap can only be increased
claims.sourceSpan: The thirty hours may be increased by the adoption of a motion

claims.claim: Cloture ends debate without rejecting the matter being debated
claims.sourceSpan: is the only procedure by which the Senate can vote to set an end to a debate without also rejecting the bill, amendment, conference report, motion, or other matter it has been debating

claims.claim: Cloture lives in paragraph 2 of Senate Rule XXII
claims.sourceSpan: The only Senate rule that permits the body, by vote, to bring consideration of a matter to an end is paragraph 2 of Rule XXII, known as the cloture rule

claims.claim: CRS states the three cloture thresholds together
claims.sourceSpan: The majority required to invoke cloture for most business is three-fifths of the Senators duly chosen and sworn, or 60 votes if there are no vacancies in the Senate's membership. However, invoking cloture on a measure or motion to amend the Senate's standing rules requires the votes of two-thirds of the Senators present and voting, or 67 votes if all 100 Senators vote. Additionally, under precedents established on November 21, 2013, and April 6, 2017, invoking cloture on presidential nominations requires a vote of a majority of Senators present and voting, or 51 votes if all 100 Senators vote

claims.claim: The 1975 change: from two-thirds of senators voting to three-fifths of all senators duly chosen and sworn, 60 of 100
claims.sourceSpan: In 1975 the Senate reduced the number of votes required for cloture from two-thirds of senators voting to three-fifths of all senators duly chosen and sworn, or 60 of the 100-member Senate

claims.claim: A cloture motion must be signed by sixteen Senators
claims.sourceSpan: signed by sixteen Senators

claims.claim: A senator may interrupt another to present the motion, and the clerk reads it
claims.sourceSpan: To present a cloture motion, a Senator may interrupt another Senator who is speaking. When the motion is presented, the clerk reads it

claims.claim: The motion lies over until the second calendar day of session, with worked examples for Monday and Friday filings
claims.sourceSpan: lies over until the second calendar day on which the Senate is in session. For example, if the motion is filed on Monday, it lies over until Wednesday, assuming the Senate is in session daily. If the motion is filed on Friday, it lies over until Tuesday unless the Senate was in session on Saturday or Sunday

claims.claim: Rule XXII: the motion is laid before the Senate one hour after it meets on the following calendar day but one
claims.sourceSpan: one hour after the Senate meets on the following calendar day but one

claims.claim: The time for the cloture vote may be changed by unanimous consent and the quorum call is routinely waived
claims.sourceSpan: The time for the cloture vote may be changed by unanimous consent, and the required quorum call is routinely waived

claims.claim: The threshold is measured against the full membership: 60 votes if there are no vacancies, so vacancies lower the number
claims.sourceSpan: 60 votes if there are no vacancies in the Senate's membership

claims.claim: After cloture, no more than thirty hours of consideration of the matter on which cloture was invoked
claims.sourceSpan: no more than thirty hours of consideration of the measure, motion, or other matter on which cloture has been invoked

claims.claim: After that, the Senate proceeds without further debate to vote on final disposition
claims.sourceSpan: the Senate shall proceed, without any further debate on any question, to vote on the final disposition thereof

claims.claim: The thirty hours may be INCREASED by the adoption of a motion (first half of the quoted rule sentence; the stored text carries a page-break marker mid-sentence)
claims.sourceSpan: The thirty hours may be increased by the adoption of a motion

claims.claim: The increase is decided without debate by a three-fifths affirmative vote of the Senators duly chosen and sworn (second half of the same rule sentence)
claims.sourceSpan: decided without debate, by a three-fifths affirmative vote of the Senators duly chosen and sworn

claims.claim: Only one motion to extend time may be made in any one calendar day
claims.sourceSpan: only one motion to extend time, specified above, may be made in any one calendar day

claims.claim: There is no limit on the number of cloture votes on the same matter
claims.sourceSpan: there is no limit on the number of times that the Senate can vote on motions to invoke cloture on a bill, amendment, or other matter it is considering

claims.claim: After a defeated motion the majority leader may enter a motion to reconsider and obtain a second cloture vote later
claims.sourceSpan: Should a cloture motion be defeated, the majority leader may enter a motion to reconsider the cloture vote. This allows the majority leader to call up the motion at a subsequent time when he feels he has the votes and thereby obtain an immediate second vote on cloture

claims.claim: Amendments must be pre-filed unless every senator agrees otherwise: first degree by 1 p.m. the day after filing, second degree at least an hour before the cloture vote
claims.sourceSpan: Except by unanimous consent, no amendment shall be proposed after the vote to bring the debate to a close, unless it had been submitted in writing to the Journal Clerk by 1 o'clock p.m. on the day following the filing of the cloture motion if an amendment in the first degree, and unless it had been so submitted at least one hour prior to the beginning of the cloture vote if an amendment in the second degree

claims.claim: No dilatory motion, dilatory amendment, or non-germane amendment is in order after cloture
claims.sourceSpan: No dilatory motion, or dilatory amendment, or amendment not germane shall be in order

claims.claim: Invoking cloture on a bill kills a pending non-germane amendment its supporters favour
claims.sourceSpan: if the Senate invokes cloture on a bill, the presiding officer immediately rules on whether any pending amendment is germane. If the amendment is not germane, it falls and is ineligible for further consideration. If the Senators who wish to expedite passage of a bill also support a pending non-germane amendment to the bill, they cannot invoke cloture on the bill without also killing the amendment they favor

claims.claim: The alternative is cloture on the amendment, which can require a second cloture vote on the bill as amended
claims.sourceSpan: The alternative is to ask the Senate to invoke cloture on the amendment, not on the bill. Doing so protects the amendment from becoming subject to the germaneness requirement. After the Senate agrees to the amendment, however, it may be necessary for the Senate to invoke cloture a second time

claims.claim: Cloture on a measure to amend the standing rules requires two-thirds of the Senators present and voting
claims.sourceSpan: two-thirds of the Senators present and voting

claims.claim: The Senate adopted new precedents in the 2010s to allow a simple majority to end debate on nominations
claims.sourceSpan: The Senate adopted new precedents in the 2010s to allow a simple majority to end debate on nominations

claims.claim: November 21, 2013: reinterpretation covering all nominations except the Supreme Court
claims.sourceSpan: the Senate reinterpreted the cloture rule to lower the threshold for invoking cloture for all nominations except to the Supreme Court

claims.claim: April 6, 2017: reinterpretation extended to Supreme Court nominations
claims.sourceSpan: reinterpreted Rule XXII to allow a majority of Senators voting, a quorum being present, to invoke cloture on nominations to the U.S. Supreme Court

claims.claim: Proceedings of this kind have been called the nuclear option

claims.claim: So called because they required actions arguably at variance with established principles underlying Senate procedure
claims.sourceSpan: because they required actions arguably at variance with established principles underlying Senate procedure

claims.claim: Neither precedent removed the need to invoke cloture on a nomination
claims.sourceSpan: Importantly, neither the 2013 nor the 2017 precedent removed the potential need to invoke cloture on a nomination to reach a vote. The process for invoking cloture on a nomination remains the same

claims.claim: Final approval of a nomination is subject to a simple majority vote of its own
claims.sourceSpan: subject to a simple majority vote

claims.claim: Filibusters remain part of Senate practice, but only on legislation

claims.claim: REMOVED, the batch shared defect and this page’s worst finding (sweep F-FAIL, independently re-confirmed): "In 2013, the Senate Democratic majority changed its rules - through a simple majority vote, the nuclear option - to require only a simple majority (51 votes) to invoke cloture on executive branch nominations and lower federal court nominations. In 2017, the Senate Republican majority extended this change to Supreme Court nominations." Rule XXII paragraph 2 requires two-thirds of Senators present and voting to invoke cloture on a measure to amend the standing rules, and in the current Senate Manual (S. Doc. 118-1) the paragraph still carries only the S. Res. 28 (Feb. 27, 1986) amendment footnote. The Senate calls the 2010s actions "new precedents"; CRS R44819 describes both as reinterpretations effected by overturning a ruling of the chair. Replaced with the dated CRS account. The identical sentence in senate-filibuster.html is fixed in the same batch.

REMOVED, F-FAIL direction inversion found in this audit, not by the sweep (the sweep graded it F-UNSOURCED): "the 30 hours can be waived by unanimous consent or a three-fifths vote". Rule XXII provides the opposite - "The thirty hours may be increased by the adoption of a motion, decided without debate, by a three-fifths affirmative vote of the Senators duly chosen and sworn", with only one such motion per calendar day. No stored source supports a three-fifths waiver, and none supports a unanimous-consent waiver of the 30 hours (98-425’s unanimous-consent sentence is about the timing of the cloture VOTE, and is now quoted in its own place).

REMOVED, F-FAIL found in this audit: "In the 1960s and 1970s, the Senate filed a handful of cloture motions per year." True of the 1960s (4, 4, 7, 6, 7 per Congress) and false of the 1970s, where the Senate’s own table records 24, 44, 39, 23 and 30 per Congress. Replaced with the table rows themselves.

REMOVED, unsourced: "By the 2010s, cloture was being filed on virtually every major piece of legislation, and sometimes multiple times on the same bill." The Senate table counts motions, not the share of bills they cover, and CRS warns directly against reading cloture activity as filibuster activity. The multiple-filings half is kept where a source states it (98-425 on repeat cloture votes and on cloture on an amendment then on the bill as amended).

REMOVED, unsourced characterisation: "The frequency reflects the procedural arms race between majorities seeking to advance their agenda and minorities using every available tool to slow them down." Replaced with CRS RL30360’s own explanation - cloture as a normal floor-management tool - and 98-425’s file-and-withdraw practice.

REMOVED, F-FAIL: "All judicial and executive nominations now require only 51 votes to advance." CRS states the requirement as a majority of Senators PRESENT AND VOTING, which is 51 only if all 100 vote, and adds that the precedents did not remove the cloture step. Replaced with the CRS wording.

REMOVED in full, unsourced behavioural narrative with no named example: the section "Why Senators Vote for Cloture Against Their Own Position on the Bill" - "Majority leaders sometimes negotiate process votes separately from policy votes", "a senator might support the bill substantively but vote against cloture to protest the lack of amendment opportunities", "Cloture votes sometimes reveal cross-cutting coalitions that don’t neatly map onto support for the underlying legislation." Replaced with a sourced section on what cloture does to amendments, which gives the same reader takeaway from Rule XXII and CRS 98-425 instead of from assertion.

REMOVED, wrong threshold: "the practical requirement that most significant legislation needs 60 senators to pass, not just 51." Sixty is the threshold to END DEBATE; passage is a separate vote. Also unsourced as an empirical claim about "most significant legislation".

REMOVED, unsourced: "If cloture fails, debate continues indefinitely, and the Majority Leader typically pulls the bill from the floor rather than allow it to stall indefinitely", and "it can be brought back at any time, sometimes weeks or months later when political circumstances change." Replaced with 98-425 on the unlimited number of cloture votes and the motion to reconsider.

REPLACED, imprecise: "Vacancies reduce the required number proportionally." Three-fifths of the seats filled is not a proportional reduction of 60 in the ordinary sense; the page now states the rule the way CRS does - 60 votes if there are no vacancies - and says vacancies lower the number.

CROSS-PAGE CONSISTENCY FIX, found in the main thread by reading the freshly audited appropriations-process explainer rather than by any verifier. Both this page and its sibling said, in effect, that vacancies lower the cloture number. That is wrong for the FIRST vacancy: three-fifths of 99 is 59.4, which rounds up to 60. CRS R47106 - already stored, and the source the audited appropriations-process page quotes for exactly this threshold - states it precisely as "a vote of three-fifths of all Senators (60 votes if there is no more than one vacancy)". Both pages now carry that formulation, so all three audited pages agree. Also from cloture round 2 (0 BLOCKING, 2 ADVISORY, both LEDGER-GAP, both accepted): a row now covers the "a majority overturned a ruling of the chair" mechanism, receipted to R44819's account of the 48-52 appeal vote; and the phrase "a documented reason a senator who supports a bill might still vote against ending debate" was reworded to "a structural reason", because CRS documents the dilemma, not an instance of a senator voting that way. Round 2 also independently re-confirmed the 117th/116th column reading, the honesty of the page-break span split, and that all ten removed.* rows describe text genuinely gone from the draft.
